+# Case study: emptying an apartment in 45 days
+
+Sixteen items, a two-bedroom apartment in Denver Tech Center, one departure date. The catalog
+opened on 2026-09-25 and the last item left on 2026-11-09: **45 days**. Nothing went to the
+dumpster.
+
+| | |
+|---|---|
+| Items placed | **16 of 16** |
+| Sold | **10** |
+| Given away | **6** |
+| Left behind or thrown away | **0** |
+| Recovered against the asking prices | **86 %** |
+| Median days to sell, household items | **15 days** |
+
+The figures come from `make retro`, which adds up the targets, the reserve floors and the realized
+price of every sale from the encrypted seller record. Absolute amounts are not published; the
+percentages and the days are, because they are the part that transfers to another move. Run in
+the repository, on the day this page was last touched, it is the authority on every number here.
+
+## What the plan said, and what happened
+
+The preparation was a written price plan, not intuition: each household item carried a researched
+target (what it should fetch, from a pricing pass on 2026-09-25) and a reserve floor (the price
+below which it would be given away rather than sold). The household deadline was 2026-10-23 and
+the car's was 2026-11-09.
+
+Against those targets the household items recovered **65 %**. Against their own reserve floors they
+recovered **81 %** — below the floors in aggregate, because six items ended at zero. The car
+recovered **88 %** of its asking price and **exactly 100 %** of its floor.
+
+That is the honest reading of the sale, and it is the interesting one:
+
+- **The plan was met, the price research was optimistic.** Everything left the apartment by its
+  deadline and nothing was abandoned, which is what the plan was for. But furniture sold for about
+  two thirds of the researched expectation. A used sofa, a bed, a desk and a chair in a city with a
+  constant churn of departing renters are worth less than a listing price suggests, and each week
+  they sit they are worth less still.
+- **The car carried the result, and its floor was the only honest number in its listing.** It sold
+  on the last day of its window, at the reserve floor set for instant offers. The asking price was
+  a wish; the floor was the expectation. On the next sale, the floor would be the number in the
+  listing and the wishing would stop.
+- **The giveaways were the plan working, not the plan failing.** Four of the six items that left
+  without money went in the final days, inside the giveaway window that had been written down in
+  advance. Choosing to give something away on a fixed date is a decision; discovering on moving day
+  that it must be abandoned is not. Six of sixteen is a normal rate for furniture at this end of
+  its life.
+
+## What made the difference
+
+- **A deadline per class of item, written down.** Household items by 2026-10-23, the car by
+  2026-11-09. Two dates, two campaigns, no negotiation with a single date that everything slides
+  past.
+- **A price schedule rather than renegotiation.** One drop, then the reserve floors, then a
+  giveaway window, each opening on a date fixed in advance. Deciding the drop dates in September
+  meant not arguing with each buyer in October.
+- **One record of what was true.** Every item's status, its asking price and its realized price
+  lived in one place that both the public page and the seller's tools read, so what buyers saw
+  and what the plan said could not drift apart.
+
+## What was built for it
+
+A static bilingual catalog generated from a single YAML inventory, with a photo pipeline that
+strips location metadata, share pages per item for each marketplace, a printable building flyer
+with its own QR code, a private seller panel for repricing and posting, and a decommission path
+that ends the sale on schedule and leaves one page behind. The repository, its decisions and its
+44 lessons are public: see the [README](../README.md).
+
+## If you are doing this yourself
+
+The method is not a secret and the code is forkable. What it buys is the unglamorous part: one
+inventory, one price plan with fixed dates, one page that buyers can check at 11 pm, and an end
+that happens on time. Write to the address on [the site](https://leaving-denver.pages.dev) if you
+want it built for your move.

+# Lesson 043 — A Percentage of a Mixed Total Hides the Group That Missed
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-09
+**Tags:** [reporting, aggregation, honesty, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The close-out aggregate (`leaving-denver retro`, OPS-018) compared what the sale realized against
+what it had expected, and the first total it printed was **99 %**. That number was true, and it
+was the most misleading figure of the whole sale.
+
+Split by group it read differently: the household items recovered **65 %** of their researched
+targets and **81 %** of their own reserve floors, while the car recovered exactly **100 %** of its
+floor and brought in 96 % of the money. Two misses in opposite directions — six items at zero on
+one side, a car at its floor on the other — summed to a number that described neither.
+
+The same file produced a second, worse figure in the same run: **1753 %**. That one was not a
+judgement call but a bug. The household group's *whole* money was being divided by the targets of
+the *thirteen* items that had a target, while the numerator also held money from items that had
+none (the car had no researched target and the bed listed too late to get one). Numerator and
+denominator covered different populations, so the ratio was not a percentage of anything.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+An aggregate is the first thing anyone reads and the last thing anyone checks. Here it would have
+gone into a public page as the headline of a sale, and it would have been technically accurate: no
+figure was fudged, every input was real. The error was entirely in what was being compared with
+what.
+
+It also failed in the direction that hides work: 99 % says "the plan was right", when what actually
+happened is "the plan was met and the price research was 35 % high on furniture". The second
+sentence is the one that improves the next sale.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **Compare like with like, in code, not in prose.** When a ratio is computed over a subset —
+  the items that have a target, the rows that have a duration — sum the numerator over that same
+  subset, and keep it as its own field (`on_expected` beside `realized`). A comment saying "the
+  expected value covers those items only" is not a guard.
+- **Print the denominator's population beside the percentage.** The report shows `$627 (13)` —
+  the sum and how many items it covers. A percentage with no visible base invites exactly this
+  error.
+- **Never publish one aggregate for a sale with more than one class of item.** The end page and
+  the case study state the split (household against targets; the car against its own floor) and
+  leave the blended total out, or name it as a blend.
+- **When two classes cancel out, say so first.** The headline is not "99 % of expected"; it is
+  "the car carried the result, and the furniture came in a third below its researched price".

+# Lesson 044 — A Test Only the Deploy Job Runs Is First Tested in Production
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-10
+**Tags:** [ci, testing, deploy, secrets, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The merge that turned the site into the end page (`#268`, OPS-018) was green on the pull request
+and **red in the deploy job**: one assertion, and the deploy stopped. Production kept serving the
+catalog — the old page, with the phone number in it — for as long as it took to notice.
+
+The test was `test_the_real_envelope_passes_validation_and_is_only_in_the_seller_page`. It is
+skipped unless `SELLER_SEALED` is set (`"only the deploy job holds the real envelope"`), and the
+deploy job is the only place that secret exists. So it ran for the first time on `main`, on the
+first change that altered the shape of the build: with the sale over there is no `/seller/` to
+hold the envelope, and `[] == ['seller/index.html']` failed.
+
+Two earlier layers could have caught it and structurally could not:
+
+- The `test` job has no secret, so the test skips.
+- The `test-end-of-sale` job has no secret either, so it skips there too — the one job whose whole

+# ADR-013: The End Page States the Result
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted. It amends ADR-008 (the end page was kept, and meant to be final and empty) and relies
+on ADR-002 (a phone number is never served), ADR-004 (link-preview crawlers stay allowed) and
+ADR-010 (`noindex` and the security headers).
+
+## Date
+
+2026-11-09
+
+## Context
+
+ADR-008 kept the Pages project alive after the sale, for one reason: the links already in
+circulation (the building flyer's QR code, shared cards in chats, marketplace listings) point at
+`leaving-denver.pages.dev`, and a deleted project frees that name for anyone to claim. What it
+decided to serve was a courtesy page — "the sale is over, thank you" — and it declared that page
+final, since the deploy token dies with the credentials on 2026-11-15.
+
+The sale is over now. Sixteen items left the apartment in 45 days, and the repository holds the
+whole record of how: the researched targets, the reserve floors, the realized price and the day of
+every sale. The page that outlives all of it carried none of that. The only artefact most visitors
+will ever see — and the only one that survives the repository's own archive — said nothing about
+what had happened, what it recovered, or who had built it.
+
+One offer was considered and rejected: telling a visitor that "this space could be yours". It is
+not possible — a `pages.dev` subdomain belongs to the Cloudflare account that owns the project and
+cannot be transferred — and it is the precise risk ADR-008 was written against, since the whole
+point of keeping the name was that no third party ever answers those old links. What can be
+offered honestly is the same construction, or the method to repeat it.
+

+
+- **The end page states the result**, in both languages: the counts (derived from
+  `data/inventory.yaml` at build time — never typed), the days and the recovered percentage, and
+  one contact line (the public alias already in the inventory's `seller` block, and the GitHub
+  profile).

+  only exist encrypted, and the end build holds no private data by design (OPS-011 AC4), so they
+  live in the locale files beside a comment naming `make retro` and the day it produced them.
+  `lesson-011` says derive figures rather than type them; here the alternative is publishing
+  private data, so the figure is typed and its source is written next to it.
+- **The offer is the construction, not the address.** "Written for one move: if you are moving and
+  want the same, or you want to run it yourself, write to me." The repository is the proof and the
+  fork; the address is never offered.
+- **Every property ADR-008 protected is kept**: no phone and no `sms:`/`tel:` link, no item, no
+  photo, no metrics beacon, `noindex` as before, and the project stays in the account and in
+  Terraform with `prevent_destroy`.

+  hand. That consequence is ADR-008's, unchanged; this decision is shipped before the deadline
+  because of it.
+

+
+### Positive
+
+- The one artefact that outlives the sale says something true and useful: how long it took, how
+  much of the asking price came back, and how to reach the person who built it.
+- The counts cannot drift, because the build reads them from the inventory; a test asserts the
+  published counts against that file, and another asserts the two languages publish the same
+  figures.
+- The result is stated in percentages and days, so the page is honest about a sale whose absolute
+  numbers are private (`data/private.sops.yaml`), and the case study can carry the same figures.
+
+### Negative
+
+- The end page now has a second audience — someone who may want this built for their own move —
+  on a page whose primary job is to tell an old link's visitor that the sale is over. The page is
+  ordered so the truth comes first and the offer last, but it is a compromise.

+  their provenance comment and the `make retro` run recorded in the spec's `verification.md`; no
+  test can close it, and pretending otherwise would be worse than naming it.

+  DuckDuckGo alias, already public in that block, not the personal address in the private file.
+

+
+- The published percentages (86 % of asking, 65 % of the researched targets, 81 % of the reserve
+  floors) are the aggregate; the case study explains the split, and `make retro` produces both for
+  whoever reads them next.

+  recorded as a sale with a realized price of `0` — correct for the lifecycle (FEAT-006), useless
+  for a published count.

+# Case study: emptying an apartment in 45 days
+
+Sixteen items, a two-bedroom apartment in Denver Tech Center, one departure date. The catalog
+opened on 2026-09-25 and the last item left on 2026-11-09: **45 days**. Nothing went to the
+dumpster.
+
+| | |
+|---|---|
+| Items placed | **16 of 16** |
+| Sold | **10** |
+| Given away | **6** |
+| Left behind or thrown away | **0** |
+| Recovered against the asking prices | **86 %** |
+| Median days to sell, household items | **15 days** |
+
+The figures come from `make retro`, which adds up the targets, the reserve floors and the realized
+price of every sale from the encrypted seller record. Absolute amounts are not published; the
+percentages and the days are, because they are the part that transfers to another move. Run in
+the repository, on the day this page was last touched, it is the authority on every number here.
+
+## What the plan said, and what happened
+
+The preparation was a written price plan, not intuition: each household item carried a researched
+target (what it should fetch, from a pricing pass on 2026-09-25) and a reserve floor (the price
+below which it would be given away rather than sold). The household deadline was 2026-10-23 and
+the car's was 2026-11-09.
+
+Against those targets the household items recovered **65 %**. Against their own reserve floors they
+recovered **81 %** — below the floors in aggregate, because six items ended at zero. The car
+recovered **88 %** of its asking price and **exactly 100 %** of its floor.
+
+That is the honest reading of the sale, and it is the interesting one:
+
+- **The plan was met, the price research was optimistic.** Everything left the apartment by its
+  deadline and nothing was abandoned, which is what the plan was for. But furniture sold for about
+  two thirds of the researched expectation. A used sofa, a bed, a desk and a chair in a city with a
+  constant churn of departing renters are worth less than a listing price suggests, and each week
+  they sit they are worth less still.
+- **The car carried the result, and its floor was the only honest number in its listing.** It sold
+  on the last day of its window, at the reserve floor set for instant offers. The asking price was
+  a wish; the floor was the expectation. On the next sale, the floor would be the number in the
+  listing and the wishing would stop.
+- **The giveaways were the plan working, not the plan failing.** Four of the six items that left
+  without money went in the final days, inside the giveaway window that had been written down in
+  advance. Choosing to give something away on a fixed date is a decision; discovering on moving day
+  that it must be abandoned is not. Six of sixteen is a normal rate for furniture at this end of
+  its life.
+
+## What made the difference
+
+- **A deadline per class of item, written down.** Household items by 2026-10-23, the car by
+  2026-11-09. Two dates, two campaigns, no negotiation with a single date that everything slides
+  past.
+- **A price schedule rather than renegotiation.** One drop, then the reserve floors, then a
+  giveaway window, each opening on a date fixed in advance. Deciding the drop dates in September
+  meant not arguing with each buyer in October.
+- **One record of what was true.** Every item's status, its asking price and its realized price
+  lived in one place that both the public page and the seller's tools read, so what buyers saw
+  and what the plan said could not drift apart.
+
+## What was built for it
+
+A static bilingual catalog generated from a single YAML inventory, with a photo pipeline that
+strips location metadata, share pages per item for each marketplace, a printable building flyer
+with its own QR code, a private seller panel for repricing and posting, and a decommission path
+that ends the sale on schedule and leaves one page behind. The repository, its decisions and its
+44 lessons are public: see the [README](../README.md).
+
+## If you are doing this yourself
+
+The method is not a secret and the code is forkable. What it buys is the unglamorous part: one
+inventory, one price plan with fixed dates, one page that buyers can check at 11 pm, and an end
+that happens on time. Write to the address on [the site](https://leaving-denver.pages.dev) if you
+want it built for your move.

+# Lesson 043 — A Percentage of a Mixed Total Hides the Group That Missed
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-09
+**Tags:** [reporting, aggregation, honesty, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The close-out aggregate (`leaving-denver retro`, OPS-018) compared what the sale realized against
+what it had expected, and the first total it printed was **99 %**. That number was true, and it
+was the most misleading figure of the whole sale.
+
+Split by group it read differently: the household items recovered **65 %** of their researched
+targets and **81 %** of their own reserve floors, while the car recovered exactly **100 %** of its
+floor and brought in 96 % of the money. Two misses in opposite directions — six items at zero on
+one side, a car at its floor on the other — summed to a number that described neither.
+
+The same file produced a second, worse figure in the same run: **1753 %**. That one was not a
+judgement call but a bug. The household group's *whole* money was being divided by the targets of
+the *thirteen* items that had a target, while the numerator also held money from items that had
+none (the car had no researched target and the bed listed too late to get one). Numerator and
+denominator covered different populations, so the ratio was not a percentage of anything.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+An aggregate is the first thing anyone reads and the last thing anyone checks. Here it would have
+gone into a public page as the headline of a sale, and it would have been technically accurate: no
+figure was fudged, every input was real. The error was entirely in what was being compared with
+what.
+
+It also failed in the direction that hides work: 99 % says "the plan was right", when what actually
+happened is "the plan was met and the price research was 35 % high on furniture". The second
+sentence is the one that improves the next sale.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **Compare like with like, in code, not in prose.** When a ratio is computed over a subset —
+  the items that have a target, the rows that have a duration — sum the numerator over that same
+  subset, and keep it as its own field (`on_expected` beside `realized`). A comment saying "the
+  expected value covers those items only" is not a guard.
+- **Print the denominator's population beside the percentage.** The report shows `$627 (13)` —
+  the sum and how many items it covers. A percentage with no visible base invites exactly this
+  error.
+- **Never publish one aggregate for a sale with more than one class of item.** The end page and
+  the case study state the split (household against targets; the car against its own floor) and
+  leave the blended total out, or name it as a blend.
+- **When two classes cancel out, say so first.** The headline is not "99 % of expected"; it is
+  "the car carried the result, and the furniture came in a third below its researched price".

+# Lesson 044 — A Test Only the Deploy Job Runs Is First Tested in Production
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-10
+**Tags:** [ci, testing, deploy, secrets, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The merge that turned the site into the end page (`#268`, OPS-018) was green on the pull request
+and **red in the deploy job**: one assertion, and the deploy stopped. Production kept serving the
+catalog — the old page, with the phone number in it — for as long as it took to notice.
+
+The test was `test_the_real_envelope_passes_validation_and_is_only_in_the_seller_page`. It is
+skipped unless `SELLER_SEALED` is set (`"only the deploy job holds the real envelope"`), and the
+deploy job is the only place that secret exists. So it ran for the first time on `main`, on the
+first change that altered the shape of the build: with the sale over there is no `/seller/` to
+hold the envelope, and `[] == ['seller/index.html']` failed.
+
+Two earlier layers could have caught it and structurally could not:
+
+- The `test` job has no secret, so the test skips.
+- The `test-end-of-sale` job has no secret either, so it skips there too — the one job whose whole
+  purpose is the end build.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+"CI is green" means *the jobs that ran* passed. A test gated on a production-only secret is not in
+that set, so every assertion it makes about the built artefact is verified for the first time
+against the thing that ships. Here the artefact that ships was a page that had stopped being
+served, and the cost of the discovery was production serving a phone number that is being closed
+on 2026-11-15.
+
+The failure was also *good news in disguise*: the assertion was right in spirit and only wrong
+about which build it was reading. What was missing was not a guard but a way for a pre-merge job
+to run it.
+

+  sibling test that already used a throwaway envelope built a *catalog* scratch — its helper drops

+  exist in one of them only.
+- **A test's expectation may depend on the build mode; the mode must be an input, not an
+  assumption.** `[] if sale_is_over() else ["seller/index.html"]` is honest and checkable; a bare
+  `["seller/index.html"]` is an assumption about a sale that is in progress.
+- **When a job only runs on `main`, treat its first run as a code review of itself.** Either move
+  the assertion earlier (a scratch build, a fixture, a synthetic secret) or accept, out loud, that
+  production is where it gets tested.
+- **Green on the PR is a claim about the jobs that ran.** Say which ones when it matters, and never
+  merge a change that alters the shipped artefact's shape on the strength of a job that skipped the
+  check that cares about it.

+|---|---|

+| Sold | **10** |
+| Given away | **6** |
+| Left behind or thrown away | **0** |
+| Recovered against the asking prices | **86 %** |

+# Lesson 043 — A Percentage of a Mixed Total Hides the Group That Missed
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-09
+**Tags:** [reporting, aggregation, honesty, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The close-out aggregate (`leaving-denver retro`, OPS-018) compared what the sale realized against
+what it had expected, and the first total it printed was **99 %**. That number was true, and it
+was the most misleading figure of the whole sale.
+
+Split by group it read differently: the household items recovered **65 %** of their researched
+targets and **81 %** of their own reserve floors, while the car recovered exactly **100 %** of its
+floor and brought in 96 % of the money. Two misses in opposite directions — six items at zero on
+one side, a car at its floor on the other — summed to a number that described neither.
+
+The same file produced a second, worse figure in the same run: **1753 %**. That one was not a
+judgement call but a bug. The household group's *whole* money was being divided by the targets of
+the *thirteen* items that had a target, while the numerator also held money from items that had
+none (the car had no researched target and the bed listed too late to get one). Numerator and
+denominator covered different populations, so the ratio was not a percentage of anything.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+An aggregate is the first thing anyone reads and the last thing anyone checks. Here it would have
+gone into a public page as the headline of a sale, and it would have been technically accurate: no
+figure was fudged, every input was real. The error was entirely in what was being compared with
+what.
+
+It also failed in the direction that hides work: 99 % says "the plan was right", when what actually
+happened is "the plan was met and the price research was 35 % high on furniture". The second
+sentence is the one that improves the next sale.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **Compare like with like, in code, not in prose.** When a ratio is computed over a subset —
+  the items that have a target, the rows that have a duration — sum the numerator over that same
+  subset, and keep it as its own field (`on_expected` beside `realized`). A comment saying "the
+  expected value covers those items only" is not a guard.
+- **Print the denominator's population beside the percentage.** The report shows `$627 (13)` —
+  the sum and how many items it covers. A percentage with no visible base invites exactly this
+  error.
+- **Never publish one aggregate for a sale with more than one class of item.** The end page and
+  the case study state the split (household against targets; the car against its own floor) and
+  leave the blended total out, or name it as a blend.
+- **When two classes cancel out, say so first.** The headline is not "99 % of expected"; it is
+  "the car carried the result, and the furniture came in a third below its researched price".

+# Lesson 044 — A Test Only the Deploy Job Runs Is First Tested in Production
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-10
+**Tags:** [ci, testing, deploy, secrets, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The merge that turned the site into the end page (`#268`, OPS-018) was green on the pull request
+and **red in the deploy job**: one assertion, and the deploy stopped. Production kept serving the
+catalog — the old page, with the phone number in it — for as long as it took to notice.
+
+The test was `test_the_real_envelope_passes_validation_and_is_only_in_the_seller_page`. It is
+skipped unless `SELLER_SEALED` is set (`"only the deploy job holds the real envelope"`), and the
+deploy job is the only place that secret exists. So it ran for the first time on `main`, on the
+first change that altered the shape of the build: with the sale over there is no `/seller/` to
+hold the envelope, and `[] == ['seller/index.html']` failed.
+
+Two earlier layers could have caught it and structurally could not:
+
+- The `test` job has no secret, so the test skips.
+- The `test-end-of-sale` job has no secret either, so it skips there too — the one job whose whole
+  purpose is the end build.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+"CI is green" means *the jobs that ran* passed. A test gated on a production-only secret is not in
+that set, so every assertion it makes about the built artefact is verified for the first time
+against the thing that ships. Here the artefact that ships was a page that had stopped being
+served, and the cost of the discovery was production serving a phone number that is being closed
+on 2026-11-15.
+
+The failure was also *good news in disguise*: the assertion was right in spirit and only wrong
+about which build it was reading. What was missing was not a guard but a way for a pre-merge job
+to run it.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **A test that reads the shipped artefact must be runnable before the merge.** If it needs a
+  secret, synthesize the secret's *shape* instead: `seal_fixture()` produces a real envelope for a
+  throwaway passphrase, and one test now builds both modes with one and asserts the invariant.
+- **Synthesizing the secret is not enough if the expectation only exists in the deploy job.** The
+  sibling test that already used a throwaway envelope built a *catalog* scratch — its helper drops
+  the switch — so it could never have seen the end-mode expectation, and it passed while the
+  deploy job failed. The expectation has to be **one definition** (`expected_envelope_holders`)
+  that the pre-merge test and the deploy-only test both call; then a mode-blind assertion cannot
+  exist in one of them only.
+- **A test's expectation may depend on the build mode; the mode must be an input, not an
+  assumption.** `[] if sale_is_over() else ["seller/index.html"]` is honest and checkable; a bare
+  `["seller/index.html"]` is an assumption about a sale that is in progress.
+- **When a job only runs on `main`, treat its first run as a code review of itself.** Either move
+  the assertion earlier (a scratch build, a fixture, a synthetic secret) or accept, out loud, that
+  production is where it gets tested.
+- **Green on the PR is a claim about the jobs that ran.** Say which ones when it matters, and never
+  merge a change that alters the shipped artefact's shape on the strength of a job that skipped the
+  check that cares about it.

+# ADR-013: The End Page States the Result
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted. It amends ADR-008 (the end page was kept, and meant to be final and empty) and relies
+on ADR-002 (a phone number is never served), ADR-004 (link-preview crawlers stay allowed) and
+ADR-010 (`noindex` and the security headers).
+
+## Date
+
+2026-11-09
+
+## Context
+
+ADR-008 kept the Pages project alive after the sale, for one reason: the links already in
+circulation (the building flyer's QR code, shared cards in chats, marketplace listings) point at
+`leaving-denver.pages.dev`, and a deleted project frees that name for anyone to claim. What it
+decided to serve was a courtesy page — "the sale is over, thank you" — and it declared that page
+final, since the deploy token dies with the credentials on 2026-11-15.

+The sale is over now. Sixteen items left the apartment in 45 days, and the repository holds the
+whole record of how: the researched targets, the reserve floors, the realized price and the day of
+every sale. The page that outlives all of it carried none of that. The only artefact most visitors
+will ever see — and the only one that survives the repository's own archive — said nothing about
+what had happened, what it recovered, or who had built it.
+

+not possible — a `pages.dev` subdomain belongs to the Cloudflare account that owns the project and
+cannot be transferred — and it is the precise risk ADR-008 was written against, since the whole
+point of keeping the name was that no third party ever answers those old links. What can be
+offered honestly is the same construction, or the method to repeat it.

+  one contact line (the public alias already in the inventory's `seller` block, and the GitHub
+  profile).

+  only exist encrypted, and the end build holds no private data by design (OPS-011 AC4), so they

+  private data, so the figure is typed and its source is written next to it.

+  want the same, or you want to run it yourself, write to me." The repository is the proof and the
+  fork; the address is never offered.
+- **Every property ADR-008 protected is kept**: no phone and no `sms:`/`tel:` link, no item, no
+  photo, no metrics beacon, `noindex` as before, and the project stays in the account and in

+  recorded as a sale with a realized price of `0` — correct for the lifecycle (FEAT-006), useless
+  for a published count.

+# Lesson 044 — A Test Only the Deploy Job Runs Is First Tested in Production
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-10
+**Tags:** [ci, testing, deploy, secrets, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The merge that turned the site into the end page (`#268`, OPS-018) was green on the pull request
+and **red in the deploy job**: one assertion, and the deploy stopped. Production kept serving the
+catalog — the old page, with the phone number in it — for as long as it took to notice.
+
+The test was `test_the_real_envelope_passes_validation_and_is_only_in_the_seller_page`. It is
+skipped unless `SELLER_SEALED` is set (`"only the deploy job holds the real envelope"`), and the
+deploy job is the only place that secret exists. So it ran for the first time on `main`, on the
+first change that altered the shape of the build: with the sale over there is no `/seller/` to
+hold the envelope, and `[] == ['seller/index.html']` failed.
+
+Two earlier layers could have caught it and structurally could not:
+
+- The `test` job has no secret, so the test skips.
+- The `test-end-of-sale` job has no secret either, so it skips there too — the one job whose whole
+  purpose is the end build.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+"CI is green" means *the jobs that ran* passed. A test gated on a production-only secret is not in
+that set, so every assertion it makes about the built artefact is verified for the first time
+against the thing that ships. Here the artefact that ships was a page that had stopped being
+served, and the cost of the discovery was production serving a phone number that is being closed
+on 2026-11-15.
+
+The failure was also *good news in disguise*: the assertion was right in spirit and only wrong
+about which build it was reading. What was missing was not a guard but a way for a pre-merge job
+to run it.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **A test that reads the shipped artefact must be runnable before the merge.** If it needs a
+  secret, synthesize the secret's *shape* instead: `seal_fixture()` produces a real envelope for a
+  throwaway passphrase, and one test now builds both modes with one and asserts the invariant.
+- **Synthesizing the secret is not enough if the expectation only exists in the deploy job.** The
+  sibling test that already used a throwaway envelope built a *catalog* scratch — its helper drops
+  the switch — so it could never have seen the end-mode expectation, and it passed while the
+  deploy job failed. The expectation has to be **one definition** (`expected_envelope_holders`)
+  that the pre-merge test and the deploy-only test both call; then a mode-blind assertion cannot
+  exist in one of them only.
+- **A test's expectation may depend on the build mode; the mode must be an input, not an
+  assumption.** `[] if sale_is_over() else ["seller/index.html"]` is honest and checkable; a bare
+  `["seller/index.html"]` is an assumption about a sale that is in progress.
+- **When a job only runs on `main`, treat its first run as a code review of itself.** Either move
+  the assertion earlier (a scratch build, a fixture, a synthetic secret) or accept, out loud, that
+  production is where it gets tested.
+- **Green on the PR is a claim about the jobs that ran.** Say which ones when it matters, and never
+  merge a change that alters the shipped artefact's shape on the strength of a job that skipped the
+  check that cares about it.

+---
+id: "ADR-013-the-end-page-states-the-result"
+type: adr
+status: accepted
+owner: manu

+
+# ADR-013: The End Page States the Result
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted. It amends ADR-008 (the end page was kept, and meant to be final and empty) and relies
+on ADR-002 (a phone number is never served), ADR-004 (link-preview crawlers stay allowed) and
+ADR-010 (`noindex` and the security headers).
+
+## Date
+
+2026-11-09
+
+## Context
+
+ADR-008 kept the Pages project alive after the sale, for one reason: the links already in
+circulation (the building flyer's QR code, shared cards in chats, marketplace listings) point at
+`leaving-denver.pages.dev`, and a deleted project frees that name for anyone to claim. What it
+decided to serve was a courtesy page — "the sale is over, thank you" — and it declared that page
+final, since the deploy token dies with the credentials on 2026-11-15.
+
+The sale is over now. Sixteen items left the apartment in 45 days, and the repository holds the
+whole record of how: the researched targets, the reserve floors, the realized price and the day of
+every sale. The page that outlives all of it carried none of that. The only artefact most visitors
+will ever see — and the only one that survives the repository's own archive — said nothing about
+what had happened, what it recovered, or who had built it.
+
+One offer was considered and rejected: telling a visitor that "this space could be yours". It is
+not possible — a `pages.dev` subdomain belongs to the Cloudflare account that owns the project and
+cannot be transferred — and it is the precise risk ADR-008 was written against, since the whole
+point of keeping the name was that no third party ever answers those old links. What can be
+offered honestly is the same construction, or the method to repeat it.
+
+## Decision
+
+- **The end page states the result**, in both languages: the counts (derived from
+  `data/inventory.yaml` at build time — never typed), the days and the recovered percentage, and
+  one contact line (the public alias already in the inventory's `seller` block, and the GitHub
+  profile).
+- **Two of those figures are typed, once.** The days and the percentage come from prices that
+  only exist encrypted, and the end build holds no private data by design (OPS-011 AC4), so they
+  live in the locale files beside a comment naming `make retro` and the day it produced them.
+  `lesson-011` says derive figures rather than type them; here the alternative is publishing
+  private data, so the figure is typed and its source is written next to it.
+- **The offer is the construction, not the address.** "Written for one move: if you are moving and
+  want the same, or you want to run it yourself, write to me." The repository is the proof and the
+  fork; the address is never offered.
+- **Every property ADR-008 protected is kept**: no phone and no `sms:`/`tel:` link, no item, no
+  photo, no metrics beacon, `noindex` as before, and the project stays in the account and in
+  Terraform with `prevent_destroy`.
+- **The page may change until 2026-11-15**, and then not again without a new API token set by
+  hand. That consequence is ADR-008's, unchanged; this decision is shipped before the deadline
+  because of it.
+
+## Consequences
+
+### Positive
+
+- The one artefact that outlives the sale says something true and useful: how long it took, how
+  much of the asking price came back, and how to reach the person who built it.
+- The counts cannot drift, because the build reads them from the inventory; a test asserts the
+  published counts against that file, and another asserts the two languages publish the same
+  figures.
+- The result is stated in percentages and days, so the page is honest about a sale whose absolute
+  numbers are private (`data/private.sops.yaml`), and the case study can carry the same figures.
+
+### Negative
+
+- The end page now has a second audience — someone who may want this built for their own move —
+  on a page whose primary job is to tell an old link's visitor that the sale is over. The page is
+  ordered so the truth comes first and the offer last, but it is a compromise.
+- Two typed figures can go stale if the encrypted record is corrected later. The mitigation is
+  their provenance comment and the `make retro` run recorded in the spec's `verification.md`; no
+  test can close it, and pretending otherwise would be worse than naming it.
+- The contact line publishes an address that was previously only in the seller data. It is the
+  DuckDuckGo alias, already public in that block, not the personal address in the private file.
+
+### Neutral
+
+- The published percentages (86 % of asking, 65 % of the researched targets, 81 % of the reserve
+  floors) are the aggregate; the case study explains the split, and `make retro` produces both for
+  whoever reads them next.
+- `disposition` is a new public item field (`sale`, or `giveaway`). It exists because a giveaway is
+  recorded as a sale with a realized price of `0` — correct for the lifecycle (FEAT-006), useless
+  for a published count.

+# Case study: emptying an apartment in 45 days
+
+Sixteen items, a two-bedroom apartment in Denver Tech Center, one departure date. The catalog
+opened on 2026-09-25 and the last item left on 2026-11-09: **45 days**. Nothing went to the
+dumpster.
+
+| | |
+|---|---|
+| Items placed | **16 of 16** |
+| Sold | **10** |
+| Given away | **6** |
+| Left behind or thrown away | **0** |
+| Recovered against the asking prices | **86 %** |
+| Median days to sell, household items | **15 days** |
+
+The figures come from `make retro`, which adds up the targets, the reserve floors and the realized
+price of every sale from the encrypted seller record. Absolute amounts are not published; the
+percentages and the days are, because they are the part that transfers to another move. Run in
+the repository, on the day this page was last touched, it is the authority on every number here.
+
+## What the plan said, and what happened
+
+The preparation was a written price plan, not intuition: each household item carried a researched
+target (what it should fetch, from a pricing pass on 2026-09-25) and a reserve floor (the price
+below which it would be given away rather than sold). The household deadline was 2026-10-23 and
+the car's was 2026-11-09.
+
+Against those targets the household items recovered **65 %**. Against their own reserve floors they
+recovered **81 %** — below the floors in aggregate, because six items ended at zero. The car
+recovered **88 %** of its asking price and **exactly 100 %** of its floor.
+
+That is the honest reading of the sale, and it is the interesting one:
+
+- **The plan was met, the price research was optimistic.** Everything left the apartment by its
+  deadline and nothing was abandoned, which is what the plan was for. But furniture sold for about
+  two thirds of the researched expectation. A used sofa, a bed, a desk and a chair in a city with a
+  constant churn of departing renters are worth less than a listing price suggests, and each week
+  they sit they are worth less still.
+- **The car carried the result, and its floor was the only honest number in its listing.** It sold
+  on the last day of its window, at the reserve floor set for instant offers. The asking price was
+  a wish; the floor was the expectation. On the next sale, the floor would be the number in the
+  listing and the wishing would stop.
+- **The giveaways were the plan working, not the plan failing.** Four of the six items that left
+  without money went in the final days, inside the giveaway window that had been written down in
+  advance. Choosing to give something away on a fixed date is a decision; discovering on moving day
+  that it must be abandoned is not. Six of sixteen is a normal rate for furniture at this end of
+  its life.
+
+## What made the difference
+
+- **A deadline per class of item, written down.** Household items by 2026-10-23, the car by
+  2026-11-09. Two dates, two campaigns, no negotiation with a single date that everything slides
+  past.
+- **A price schedule rather than renegotiation.** One drop, then the reserve floors, then a
+  giveaway window, each opening on a date fixed in advance. Deciding the drop dates in September
+  meant not arguing with each buyer in October.
+- **One record of what was true.** Every item's status, its asking price and its realized price
+  lived in one place that both the public page and the seller's tools read, so what buyers saw
+  and what the plan said could not drift apart.
+
+## What was built for it
+
+A static bilingual catalog generated from a single YAML inventory, with a photo pipeline that
+strips location metadata, share pages per item for each marketplace, a printable building flyer
+with its own QR code, a private seller panel for repricing and posting, and a decommission path
+that ends the sale on schedule and leaves one page behind. The repository, its decisions and its
+44 lessons are public: see the [README](../README.md).
+
+## If you are doing this yourself
+
+The method is not a secret and the code is forkable. What it buys is the unglamorous part: one
+inventory, one price plan with fixed dates, one page that buyers can check at 11 pm, and an end
+that happens on time. Write to the address on [the site](https://leaving-denver.pages.dev) if you
+want it built for your move.

+# Lesson 043 — A Percentage of a Mixed Total Hides the Group That Missed
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-09
+**Tags:** [reporting, aggregation, honesty, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The close-out aggregate (`leaving-denver retro`, OPS-018) compared what the sale realized against
+what it had expected, and the first total it printed was **99 %**. That number was true, and it
+was the most misleading figure of the whole sale.
+
+Split by group it read differently: the household items recovered **65 %** of their researched
+targets and **81 %** of their own reserve floors, while the car recovered exactly **100 %** of its
+floor and brought in 96 % of the money. Two misses in opposite directions — six items at zero on
+one side, a car at its floor on the other — summed to a number that described neither.
+
+The same file produced a second, worse figure in the same run: **1753 %**. That one was not a
+judgement call but a bug. The household group's *whole* money was being divided by the targets of
+the *thirteen* items that had a target, while the numerator also held money from items that had
+none (the car had no researched target and the bed listed too late to get one). Numerator and
+denominator covered different populations, so the ratio was not a percentage of anything.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+An aggregate is the first thing anyone reads and the last thing anyone checks. Here it would have
+gone into a public page as the headline of a sale, and it would have been technically accurate: no
+figure was fudged, every input was real. The error was entirely in what was being compared with
+what.
+
+It also failed in the direction that hides work: 99 % says "the plan was right", when what actually
+happened is "the plan was met and the price research was 35 % high on furniture". The second
+sentence is the one that improves the next sale.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **Compare like with like, in code, not in prose.** When a ratio is computed over a subset —
+  the items that have a target, the rows that have a duration — sum the numerator over that same
+  subset, and keep it as its own field (`on_expected` beside `realized`). A comment saying "the
+  expected value covers those items only" is not a guard.
+- **Print the denominator's population beside the percentage.** The report shows `$627 (13)` —
+  the sum and how many items it covers. A percentage with no visible base invites exactly this
+  error.
+- **Never publish one aggregate for a sale with more than one class of item.** The end page and
+  the case study state the split (household against targets; the car against its own floor) and
+  leave the blended total out, or name it as a blend.
+- **When two classes cancel out, say so first.** The headline is not "99 % of expected"; it is
+  "the car carried the result, and the furniture came in a third below its researched price".

+---
+id: "ADR-013-the-end-page-states-the-result"
+type: adr
+status: accepted
+owner: manu
+date: "2026-11-09"
+issue: "mlorentedev/leaving-denver#267"
+tags: [architecture, decision, content, operations]
+created: "2026-11-09"
+---
+
+# ADR-013: The End Page States the Result
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted. It amends ADR-008 (the end page was kept, and meant to be final and empty) and relies
+on ADR-002 (a phone number is never served), ADR-004 (link-preview crawlers stay allowed) and
+ADR-010 (`noindex` and the security headers).
+
+## Date
+
+2026-11-09
+
+## Context
+
+ADR-008 kept the Pages project alive after the sale, for one reason: the links already in
+circulation (the building flyer's QR code, shared cards in chats, marketplace listings) point at
+`leaving-denver.pages.dev`, and a deleted project frees that name for anyone to claim. What it
+decided to serve was a courtesy page — "the sale is over, thank you" — and it declared that page
+final, since the deploy token dies with the credentials on 2026-11-15.
+
+The sale is over now. Sixteen items left the apartment in 45 days, and the repository holds the
+whole record of how: the researched targets, the reserve floors, the realized price and the day of
+every sale. The page that outlives all of it carried none of that. The only artefact most visitors
+will ever see — and the only one that survives the repository's own archive — said nothing about
+what had happened, what it recovered, or who had built it.
+
+One offer was considered and rejected: telling a visitor that "this space could be yours". It is
+not possible — a `pages.dev` subdomain belongs to the Cloudflare account that owns the project and
+cannot be transferred — and it is the precise risk ADR-008 was written against, since the whole
+point of keeping the name was that no third party ever answers those old links. What can be
+offered honestly is the same construction, or the method to repeat it.
+
+## Decision
+
+- **The end page states the result**, in both languages: the counts (derived from
+  `data/inventory.yaml` at build time — never typed), the days and the recovered percentage, and
+  one contact line (the public alias already in the inventory's `seller` block, and the GitHub
+  profile).
+- **Two of those figures are typed, once.** The days and the percentage come from prices that
+  only exist encrypted, and the end build holds no private data by design (OPS-011 AC4), so they
+  live in the locale files beside a comment naming `make retro` and the day it produced them.
+  `lesson-011` says derive figures rather than type them; here the alternative is publishing
+  private data, so the figure is typed and its source is written next to it.
+- **The offer is the construction, not the address.** "Written for one move: if you are moving and
+  want the same, or you want to run it yourself, write to me." The repository is the proof and the
+  fork; the address is never offered.
+- **Every property ADR-008 protected is kept**: no phone and no `sms:`/`tel:` link, no item, no
+  photo, no metrics beacon, `noindex` as before, and the project stays in the account and in
+  Terraform with `prevent_destroy`.
+- **The page may change until 2026-11-15**, and then not again without a new API token set by
+  hand. That consequence is ADR-008's, unchanged; this decision is shipped before the deadline
+  because of it.
+
+## Consequences
+
+### Positive
+
+- The one artefact that outlives the sale says something true and useful: how long it took, how
+  much of the asking price came back, and how to reach the person who built it.
+- The counts cannot drift, because the build reads them from the inventory; a test asserts the
+  published counts against that file, and another asserts the two languages publish the same
+  figures.
+- The result is stated in percentages and days, so the page is honest about a sale whose absolute
+  numbers are private (`data/private.sops.yaml`), and the case study can carry the same figures.
+
+### Negative
+
+- The end page now has a second audience — someone who may want this built for their own move —
+  on a page whose primary job is to tell an old link's visitor that the sale is over. The page is
+  ordered so the truth comes first and the offer last, but it is a compromise.
+- Two typed figures can go stale if the encrypted record is corrected later. The mitigation is
+  their provenance comment and the `make retro` run recorded in the spec's `verification.md`; no
+  test can close it, and pretending otherwise would be worse than naming it.
+- The contact line publishes an address that was previously only in the seller data. It is the
+  DuckDuckGo alias, already public in that block, not the personal address in the private file.
+
+### Neutral
+
+- The published percentages (86 % of asking, 65 % of the researched targets, 81 % of the reserve
+  floors) are the aggregate; the case study explains the split, and `make retro` produces both for
+  whoever reads them next.
+- `disposition` is a new public item field (`sale`, or `giveaway`). It exists because a giveaway is
+  recorded as a sale with a realized price of `0` — correct for the lifecycle (FEAT-006), useless
+  for a published count.

+# Case study: emptying an apartment in 45 days
+
+Sixteen items, a two-bedroom apartment in Denver Tech Center, one departure date. The catalog
+opened on 2026-09-25 and the last item left on 2026-11-09: **45 days**. Nothing went to the
+dumpster.
+
+| | |
+|---|---|
+| Items placed | **16 of 16** |
+| Sold | **10** |
+| Given away | **6** |
+| Left behind or thrown away | **0** |
+| Recovered against the asking prices | **86 %** |
+| Median days to sell, household items | **15 days** |
+
+The figures come from `make retro`, which adds up the targets, the reserve floors and the realized
+price of every sale from the encrypted seller record. Absolute amounts are not published; the
+percentages and the days are, because they are the part that transfers to another move. Run in
+the repository, on the day this page was last touched, it is the authority on every number here.
+
+## What the plan said, and what happened
+
+The preparation was a written price plan, not intuition: each household item carried a researched
+target (what it should fetch, from a pricing pass on 2026-09-25) and a reserve floor (the price
+below which it would be given away rather than sold). The household deadline was 2026-10-23 and
+the car's was 2026-11-09.
+
+Against those targets the household items recovered **65 %**. Against their own reserve floors they
+recovered **81 %** — below the floors in aggregate, because six items ended at zero. The car
+recovered **88 %** of its asking price and **exactly 100 %** of its floor.
+
+That is the honest reading of the sale, and it is the interesting one:
+
+- **The plan was met, the price research was optimistic.** Everything left the apartment by its
+  deadline and nothing was abandoned, which is what the plan was for. But furniture sold for about
+  two thirds of the researched expectation. A used sofa, a bed, a desk and a chair in a city with a
+  constant churn of departing renters are worth less than a listing price suggests, and each week
+  they sit they are worth less still.
+- **The car carried the result, and its floor was the only honest number in its listing.** It sold
+  on the last day of its window, at the reserve floor set for instant offers. The asking price was
+  a wish; the floor was the expectation. On the next sale, the floor would be the number in the
+  listing and the wishing would stop.
+- **The giveaways were the plan working, not the plan failing.** Four of the six items that left
+  without money went in the final days, inside the giveaway window that had been written down in
+  advance. Choosing to give something away on a fixed date is a decision; discovering on moving day
+  that it must be abandoned is not. Six of sixteen is a normal rate for furniture at this end of
+  its life.
+
+## What made the difference
+
+- **A deadline per class of item, written down.** Household items by 2026-10-23, the car by
+  2026-11-09. Two dates, two campaigns, no negotiation with a single date that everything slides
+  past.
+- **A price schedule rather than renegotiation.** One drop, then the reserve floors, then a
+  giveaway window, each opening on a date fixed in advance. Deciding the drop dates in September
+  meant not arguing with each buyer in October.
+- **One record of what was true.** Every item's status, its asking price and its realized price
+  lived in one place that both the public page and the seller's tools read, so what buyers saw
+  and what the plan said could not drift apart.
+
+## What was built for it
+
+A static bilingual catalog generated from a single YAML inventory, with a photo pipeline that
+strips location metadata, share pages per item for each marketplace, a printable building flyer
+with its own QR code, a private seller panel for repricing and posting, and a decommission path
+that ends the sale on schedule and leaves one page behind. The repository, its decisions and its
+44 lessons are public: see the [README](../README.md).
+
+## If you are doing this yourself
+
+The method is not a secret and the code is forkable. What it buys is the unglamorous part: one
+inventory, one price plan with fixed dates, one page that buyers can check at 11 pm, and an end
+that happens on time. Write to the address on [the site](https://leaving-denver.pages.dev) if you
+want it built for your move.

+# Lesson 043 — A Percentage of a Mixed Total Hides the Group That Missed
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-09
+**Tags:** [reporting, aggregation, honesty, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The close-out aggregate (`leaving-denver retro`, OPS-018) compared what the sale realized against
+what it had expected, and the first total it printed was **99 %**. That number was true, and it
+was the most misleading figure of the whole sale.
+
+Split by group it read differently: the household items recovered **65 %** of their researched
+targets and **81 %** of their own reserve floors, while the car recovered exactly **100 %** of its
+floor and brought in 96 % of the money. Two misses in opposite directions — six items at zero on
+one side, a car at its floor on the other — summed to a number that described neither.
+
+The same file produced a second, worse figure in the same run: **1753 %**. That one was not a
+judgement call but a bug. The household group's *whole* money was being divided by the targets of
+the *thirteen* items that had a target, while the numerator also held money from items that had
+none (the car had no researched target and the bed listed too late to get one). Numerator and
+denominator covered different populations, so the ratio was not a percentage of anything.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+An aggregate is the first thing anyone reads and the last thing anyone checks. Here it would have
+gone into a public page as the headline of a sale, and it would have been technically accurate: no
+figure was fudged, every input was real. The error was entirely in what was being compared with
+what.
+
+It also failed in the direction that hides work: 99 % says "the plan was right", when what actually
+happened is "the plan was met and the price research was 35 % high on furniture". The second
+sentence is the one that improves the next sale.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **Compare like with like, in code, not in prose.** When a ratio is computed over a subset —
+  the items that have a target, the rows that have a duration — sum the numerator over that same
+  subset, and keep it as its own field (`on_expected` beside `realized`). A comment saying "the
+  expected value covers those items only" is not a guard.
+- **Print the denominator's population beside the percentage.** The report shows `$627 (13)` —
+  the sum and how many items it covers. A percentage with no visible base invites exactly this
+  error.
+- **Never publish one aggregate for a sale with more than one class of item.** The end page and
+  the case study state the split (household against targets; the car against its own floor) and
+  leave the blended total out, or name it as a blend.
+- **When two classes cancel out, say so first.** The headline is not "99 % of expected"; it is
+  "the car carried the result, and the furniture came in a third below its researched price".

+# Lesson 044 — A Test Only the Deploy Job Runs Is First Tested in Production
+
+**Date:** 2026-11-10
+**Tags:** [ci, testing, deploy, secrets, close-out]
+
+## What happened
+
+The merge that turned the site into the end page (`#268`, OPS-018) was green on the pull request
+and **red in the deploy job**: one assertion, and the deploy stopped. Production kept serving the
+catalog — the old page, with the phone number in it — for as long as it took to notice.
+
+The test was `test_the_real_envelope_passes_validation_and_is_only_in_the_seller_page`. It is
+skipped unless `SELLER_SEALED` is set (`"only the deploy job holds the real envelope"`), and the
+deploy job is the only place that secret exists. So it ran for the first time on `main`, on the
+first change that altered the shape of the build: with the sale over there is no `/seller/` to
+hold the envelope, and `[] == ['seller/index.html']` failed.
+
+Two earlier layers could have caught it and structurally could not:
+
+- The `test` job has no secret, so the test skips.
+- The `test-end-of-sale` job has no secret either, so it skips there too — the one job whose whole
+  purpose is the end build.
+
+## Why it matters
+
+"CI is green" means *the jobs that ran* passed. A test gated on a production-only secret is not in
+that set, so every assertion it makes about the built artefact is verified for the first time
+against the thing that ships. Here the artefact that ships was a page that had stopped being
+served, and the cost of the discovery was production serving a phone number that is being closed
+on 2026-11-15.
+
+The failure was also *good news in disguise*: the assertion was right in spirit and only wrong
+about which build it was reading. What was missing was not a guard but a way for a pre-merge job
+to run it.
+
+## Rule
+
+- **A test that reads the shipped artefact must be runnable before the merge.** If it needs a
+  secret, synthesize the secret's *shape* instead: `seal_fixture()` produces a real envelope for a
+  throwaway passphrase, and one test now builds both modes with one and asserts the invariant.
+- **Synthesizing the secret is not enough if the expectation only exists in the deploy job.** The
+  sibling test that already used a throwaway envelope built a *catalog* scratch — its helper drops
+  the switch — so it could never have seen the end-mode expectation, and it passed while the
+  deploy job failed. The expectation has to be **one definition** (`expected_envelope_holders`)
+  that the pre-merge test and the deploy-only test both call; then a mode-blind assertion cannot
+  exist in one of them only.
+- **A test's expectation may depend on the build mode; the mode must be an input, not an
+  assumption.** `[] if sale_is_over() else ["seller/index.html"]` is honest and checkable; a bare
+  `["seller/index.html"]` is an assumption about a sale that is in progress.
+- **When a job only runs on `main`, treat its first run as a code review of itself.** Either move
+  the assertion earlier (a scratch build, a fixture, a synthetic secret) or accept, out loud, that
+  production is where it gets tested.
+- **Green on the PR is a claim about the jobs that ran.** Say which ones when it matters, and never
+  merge a change that alters the shipped artefact's shape on the strength of a job that skipped the
+  check that cares about it.

content.text:
Closes #267. Spec: `specs/OPS-018-close-out/`.

## What

The sale ended on 2026-11-09 and the repository still described one in progress: six items `Available`, and nothing recording that six of the sixteen left without money changing hands (a giveaway is stored as a sale at `0`, deliberately). This closes it out in one change, and it is the last deploy the credentials allow (ADR-008: the token is revoked on 2026-11-15).

- **The data states the end.** Every item `Sold`; a new optional `disposition` (`sale` default, `giveaway`) marks the six that went without payment, so the published counts are answerable without decrypting anything. An unknown value fails the build. `status` keeps its FEAT-006 meaning.
- **The aggregate is a command.** `make retro` / `leaving-denver retro` sums the researched targets, the reserve floors and the realized price of every sale, per group and in total, and prints the counts and the days. `--json` for the machine. Absolute money stays seller-only; the output holds no phone and no token, and an unreadable private file prints no total at all.
- **The end page states the result.** Counts derived from the inventory at build time; days and recovered percentage typed once per locale with their provenance; one contact line offering the same construction — never the address, which cannot be transferred and is exactly what ADR-008 kept out of third-party hands.
- **The retrospective.** `docs/case-study.md` (percentages and days, no absolute amounts), README "Results", ADR-013 amending ADR-008, `docs/lessons/lesson-043-…`.

## The result, in percentages and days

16 items, 45 days, nothing thrown away: **10 sold, 6 given away, 86 % of the asking prices recovered**, median 15 days per household item.

Against the researched targets the household items recovered **65 %**, and **81 %** of their own reserve floors; the car recovered **exactly 100 % of its floor** on the last day of its window, and brought in 96 % of the money. So: the plan was met in full and the price research was optimistic by about a third on furniture. That split is the point, and it is why the blended "99 % of expected" is deliberately not published anywhere.

## Evidence

- `make check` with the switch on: **1183 passed, 298 skipped**, lint and `terraform validate` clean.
- Rehearsed before merging, per `docs/runbooks/decommission.md`:
  `make deploy BRANCH=candidate` then `scripts/smoke.sh` → `smoke OK (sale over)`;
  `/` and `/es/` serve the new page (`16 items · 10 sold · 45 days · 86%` / `16 artículos · 10 vendidos · 45 días · 86 %`), `/i/sofa-sleeper/` answers 302, and no page carries `sms:`/`tel:`.
- The `make retro` run the published figures came from is recorded in `specs/OPS-018-close-out/verification.md`.

## Notes for the reviewer

- The days and the percentage are **typed**, not derived: the end build holds no private data by design (OPS-011 AC4). They live in one place per language, next to a comment naming `make retro` and its date, and a test asserts both languages publish the same figures. The gap is named in ADR-013 rather than papered over.
- The switch is flipped here, so the fourteen live-catalog tests that expected items still for sale join `CATALOG_TESTS` with their reason (four also in `SKIPPED_DESPITE_ITS_NAME`, because their names mention "private" without guarding it). The catalog will not be built again.
- CI's "turn the sale off in this checkout" step is now idempotent: with the switch committed its `sed` would have written a duplicate key.

## Knowledge

- Lesson: `docs/lessons/lesson-043-a-percentage-of-a-mixed-total-hides-the-group-that-missed.md`
- ADR: `docs/adr/adr-013-the-end-page-states-the-result.md`
- Runbook: none: `docs/runbooks/decommission.md` is unchanged — the steps it orders (credentials, old deployments, monitor, digest, archive) are the owner's, and they follow this merge.
